h1: Fence Installation in Dallas, TX: Wood and Privacy Fences
heroSub: How a new or replacement 6-ft or 8-ft wood privacy fence gets measured, quoted, permitted and built by an independent Dallas contractor. Rules and prices are attributed to the city or firm that publishes them.
introHtml:
Fence installation in Dallas TX usually means one of two jobs: a new 6-ft or 8-ft wood privacy fence on a lot that never had one, or a full replacement of a fence that has leaned, greyed and lost pickets. This page covers how an installation runs from measuring to build, what the wood, post and style choices change on a quote, and what the City of Dallas says about height and permits. White Rock Fence Co is advertising that connects Dallas homeowners with independent fence contractors. It does not build fences itself.

Every price here is what one named firm publishes, or a national guide labeled as national. None of it is a quote from this site. Get two or three written quotes that list the same height, wood, posts and extras, then call (214) 555-0137 to be put in touch with an independent contractor who quotes the job.

features.title: Cedar or pine pickets
features.desc: TX Fence & Deck lists 150 lf of pressure-treated pine at $2,200 to $3,300 installed and western red cedar at $3,000 to $4,500. Ask every quote to name the wood.

features.title: Side-by-side or board-on-board
features.desc: Board-on-board overlaps the pickets so the fence stays solid. TX Fence & Deck says it adds $2 to $5 per linear foot over a basic dog-ear fence.

features.title: Posts set in concrete
features.desc: Wood or steel posts, set in concrete, carry the fence. Much of the Dallas area sits on expansive clay, so ask what the quote specifies for posts.

features.title: Top cap and trim
features.desc: A cap and trim rail finish the top edge and shed water off the pickets. Check whether they are in the base price or priced as extras.

features.title: City permit when height triggers one
features.desc: The City of Dallas requires a fence permit above 6 ft outside the front yard, and caps fences at 9 ft. Confirm with the City and your HOA before anything is built.

features.title: Tear-out and haul-off
features.desc: Taking down the old fence and hauling it away is its own line on a replacement quote. Ask whether it is included and who calls 811 before digging.

sections.heading: How a fence installation job runs
sections.html:
A job starts with a measure. The contractor walks the property line, counts linear feet and notes gates, slopes, trees, alley access, utility easements and any corner-lot sight clearance. Ask who is confirming the property line, because a fence built on the wrong side of it turns into a dispute that no quote settles.

From there the steps run in a fixed order:

  • Written quote: height, wood species, picket style, post material, cap and trim, gates, total linear feet, and separate lines for tear-out and haul-off.
  • Permit and approvals: a City permit if the height or location triggers one, plus written HOA approval where an association applies.
  • Old fence out: on a replacement, the old fence comes down and goes off site, or it stays with you. The quote should say which.
  • Build: posts set in concrete, rails, pickets, cap and trim, gates hung, and the site cleaned up.

Texas811 states that Texas law requires you or your contractor to contact 811 two business days before you dig, and that a hired contractor is responsible for making that call. Ask the contractor to confirm it before the post holes start.

sections.heading: Wood, posts and style: what changes the quote
sections.html:
Cedar versus pine. For 150 lf, TX Fence & Deck lists pressure-treated pine at $2,200 to $3,300 installed and western red cedar at $3,000 to $4,500, and says cedar typically costs 20 to 35 percent more in materials. Cedar pickets are the usual choice when the fence will be seen from the street or the neighbor's side. Pine is the budget option, so compare quotes on the same wood.

Side-by-side versus board-on-board. A basic fence sets pickets edge to edge. Board-on-board overlaps two layers, so the fence looks solid from both sides. TX Fence & Deck says board-on-board and shadow box styles typically add $2 to $5 per linear foot, while DFW Fence Contractor says board-on-board adds about 30 percent over a regular wood fence. The two firms measure it differently, so ask each bidder for the style as its own line.

Posts. Posts are where quotes quietly differ. Ask whether they are wood or steel and how they are set in concrete. Much of the Dallas area sits on expansive clay that swells and shrinks with moisture. This page gives no post depth, because the only figures we found come from contractor blogs and they conflict.

Cap, trim and finish. A top cap and trim rail are normally listed items, and stain or sealer is usually separate. TX Fence & Deck puts professional staining in DFW at $1.00 to $2.50 per linear foot on one page and $1.50 to $3.00 on another, so treat staining as a ballpark and get it written down.

sections.heading: Height, permits and HOA rules in Dallas
sections.html:
The Dallas Development Code (Sec. 51A-4.602) says a fence in a required yard may not exceed nine feet, and that in most residential districts a fence in the required front yard may not exceed four feet. The City's fence permit checklist (form 26-001, dated 6/10/2026) says a permit is required for fences over 4 ft in a front yard or over 6 ft in all other locations. By that wording an 8-ft board-on-board fence in a back or side yard needs a City permit, and a 6-ft fence there falls under the line. The City's DallasNow guide adds that historic, conservation and planned development districts have additional requirements.

The code also bans some materials, including sheet metal, corrugated metal, fiberglass panels and plywood. A fence may not sit in an easement without written approval from the agency involved, and it must leave firefighting access to the side and rear yard. On a corner lot, or beside a driveway or alley, the code restricts items between 2-1/2 ft and 8 ft tall inside a visibility triangle, so a solid fence may have to be set back.

Texas does not license fence contractors at the state level, but some cities register them, including Dallas, Richardson and Irving. The City's DallasNow guide says fence applications require you to add a general contractor as the contractor. Ask any bidder for city registration and proof of insurance, and do not take a promise for an answer. For HOAs, Texas Property Code Sec. 202.023 still lets many associations regulate the type of fencing, so get written approval before you sign.

The suburbs run their own rules. Each city below publishes an 8-ft rear-yard limit, but the permit trigger differs, so confirm with the city and your HOA:

  • Plano: a permit for a new fence; repairs under 25 percent in 12 months are exempt.
  • Garland: permit for a new fence where none existed, a corner lot, or a change in height, location or material.
  • Richardson: a permit for any fence 2-1/2 ft or taller.
  • Mesquite: a permit for any fence over 2 ft.
  • Irving: a permit for any new or replacement fence.
  • Carrollton: a permit for a new fence over 20 ft in length.

sections.heading: What installation costs and how to compare quotes
sections.html:
Dallas-area firms publish wide ranges. TX Fence & Deck says installed cedar privacy fence in DFW runs $18 to $28 per linear foot at 6 ft. Ergeon's Dallas County page lists wood fence at $38 to $48 per foot installed. DFW Fence Contractor says roughly $30 to $60 per linear foot for a standard 6-ft wood privacy fence. Those figures disagree because the wood, style and scope differ, so treat each as one firm's advertised range, not a price for your lot.

For 8 ft we could not find a Dallas firm's per-foot price. Fixr, a national guide, lists 150 lf at $2,250 to $6,000 for 6 ft and $4,500 to $12,750 for 8 ft. That is national, not Dallas, and it shows the direction: taller costs noticeably more, and in Dallas an 8-ft fence also brings the City permit described above.

To compare quotes fairly, make each bidder price the same height, wood, picket style, post material, cap and trim, gate count and tear-out. We publish no Dallas permit fee, because the City's fee schedule has no fence line item. Ask each contractor whether permit handling is in the number.

If the fence is a shared boundary, talk to your neighbor first. Texas Law Help says that where both neighbors use a fence straddling the line, both own it and share the cost of repair and replacement. That is general information, not legal advice. For the full picture see the Dallas fence cost guide, or look at fence repair, gate repair and iron fences if replacement is not the right call. Ready to start? Call (214) 555-0137.

faq.q: How much does a wood privacy fence cost to install in Dallas?
faq.a: It depends on who you ask. TX Fence & Deck advertises $18 to $28 per linear foot for a standard 6-ft cedar privacy fence in DFW, and $2,700 to $4,200 for 150 lf. Ergeon's Dallas County page lists wood fence at $38 to $48 per foot installed, and DFW Fence Contractor says roughly $30 to $60. None of these is a quote from this site, so get two or three written quotes.

faq.q: Do I need a permit for a new fence in Dallas?
faq.a: The City of Dallas permit checklist says a permit is required for fences over 4 ft in a front yard or over 6 ft in all other locations, with a 9 ft maximum. A 6-ft back-yard fence is under that line and an 8-ft one is over it. Neighboring cities differ: Irving requires a permit for any new or replacement fence, and Richardson for any fence 2-1/2 ft or taller. Confirm with the City, at (214) 948-4480 for Dallas, and with your HOA before building.

faq.q: Can I build an 8-ft privacy fence in Dallas?
faq.a: Dallas code allows fences up to 9 ft in required side and rear yards, with 4 ft the limit in the required front yard, and the City's checklist requires a permit above 6 ft. Plano, Garland, Richardson, Mesquite, Irving and Carrollton each publish an 8-ft rear-yard limit. On 150 lf, national guide Fixr lists 6 ft at $2,250 to $6,000 and 8 ft at $4,500 to $12,750, and we found no Dallas firm's 8-ft per-foot price.

faq.q: Is cedar or board-on-board worth the extra money?
faq.a: For 150 lf, TX Fence & Deck lists pressure-treated pine at $2,200 to $3,300 installed and cedar at $3,000 to $4,500. The same firm says board-on-board adds $2 to $5 per linear foot over a basic dog-ear fence, while DFW Fence Contractor says about 30 percent. Whether it pays off depends on your budget and how long you plan to stay, so ask each bidder to price both options.

faq.q: Who pays for a fence on the property line?
faq.a: Texas Law Help says that if both neighbors use a fence straddling the boundary line, both own it and share the cost of repairing and replacing it. A fence wholly on one lot belongs to that owner. At TX Fence & Deck's cedar range of $3,000 to $4,500 for 150 lf, the split matters, so agree on it in writing before the quote is signed. This is general information, not legal advice.
